An emetic is any substance — a medicine, chemical, or naturally occurring agent — that causes a person or animal to vomit when it is swallowed or administered. That's it at its heart: something that makes you throw up, either by design or as a known effect.
Why Would Anyone Want Something That Causes Vomiting?

This is the key to truly understanding the word. An emetic is almost always used with a specific, intentional purpose — not vomiting for its own sake, but vomiting as a means to an end.

The classic and most important use is poisoning or accidental ingestion of a toxic substance. If someone swallows something dangerous, getting it out of the stomach quickly — before the body absorbs it — can prevent serious harm or even death. An emetic forces the stomach to empty itself, expelling the harmful substance before it can cause damage.

Think of it like this: your stomach is a holding chamber. If something dangerous enters it, the goal is to get it out of that chamber as fast as possible. An emetic is the tool that does that.
How Does an Emetic Actually Work?

There are two main pathways by which a substance can trigger vomiting:

1. Local irritation (acting directly on the stomach)
Some emetics work by irritating the lining of the stomach. This irritation sends a distress signal to the brain, which then triggers the vomiting reflex. The stomach, in a sense, "complains" loudly enough that the brain commands it to empty itself.

2. Central action (acting on the brain)
Other emetics bypass the stomach entirely and work by stimulating a specific area of the brain called the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) — sometimes called the "vomiting center." This zone is essentially the brain's alarm system for detecting toxins in the blood. When an emetic stimulates this area, the brain sends a vomiting signal to the stomach, even if the stomach itself isn't directly irritated.

Some emetics work through both pathways simultaneously, making them more reliably effective.

Syrup of ipecac — For much of the 20th century, this was the go-to household emetic. Parents were advised to keep a bottle at home in case a child swallowed something dangerous. It works through both local stomach irritation and central brain stimulation. However, as you'll read below, it has largely fallen out of favor in modern medicine.

Apomorphine — A medically administered emetic that acts centrally (on the brain's vomiting center). It is still used in veterinary medicine and occasionally in human medicine under controlled conditions.

Hydrogen peroxide — Diluted hydrogen peroxide is commonly used by veterinarians to induce vomiting in dogs that have eaten something toxic. It works by releasing oxygen bubbles in the stomach, causing irritation.

Salt water and mustard water — Historically used as crude, home-remedy emetics. They work by irritating the stomach lining. These are generally not recommended today because of the risks involved (high sodium intake from salt water can itself be dangerous).

Certain plants and natural substances — Many plants contain compounds that act as natural emetics. In fact, some poisons are themselves emetic — the body's natural response to ingesting something toxic is often to vomit it out, which is why food poisoning frequently comes with vomiting.
The Important Shift in Modern Medicine

Here is something crucial that gives you a fuller picture of the word in its real-world context: emetics, once widely used in emergency poisoning treatment, are now largely discouraged in modern clinical medicine.

For decades, ipecac was the standard first response to accidental poisoning. But by the early 2000s, major medical organizations — including poison control centers — began recommending against its routine use, for several important reasons:

  • Corrosive substances (like bleach, strong acids, or drain cleaner) can cause severe damage to the throat and esophagus on the way down. If you force the person to vomit, the corrosive substance burns those same tissues again on the way back up, doubling the injury. Using an emetic here causes more harm.
  • Petroleum products (gasoline, lighter fluid) carry a serious risk of being accidentally inhaled into the lungs during vomiting, causing a dangerous condition called aspiration pneumonia.
  • Unconscious or semi-conscious patients cannot protect their airway while vomiting, so they risk choking or aspirating vomit into their lungs.
  • Studies also showed that emetics often don't remove as much of the ingested substance as was assumed, and by the time they were typically administered, much of the toxic substance had already moved past the stomach.

Today, activated charcoal and gastric lavage (stomach pumping) are preferred in clinical settings for poisoning cases. Activated charcoal binds to many toxic substances in the stomach and prevents them from being absorbed, without the risks of vomiting. Still, emetics retain a valid role — particularly in veterinary medicine — and understanding when not to use them is as important as understanding what they are.
Emetic vs. Antiemetic — a Key Contrast

To sharpen your understanding, consider the word's direct opposite: an antiemetic. An antiemetic is a substance that prevents or suppresses vomiting — for example, the medications given to chemotherapy patients or to people who experience severe nausea from motion sickness. Where an emetic triggers vomiting, an antiemetic blocks it. The two are mirror images of each other.

An emetic is a substance that deliberately causes vomiting, most often used to expel a swallowed poison or toxic substance from the stomach — though modern medicine now uses it far more cautiously than before, and never when certain dangerous substances like corrosives are involved.
